title: Polynomials and Factorisation
shortDescription: Degree, zeroes, remainder and factor theorems, identities and factorisation techniques.
genZNote: Factor first, panic never. The remainder theorem is the 10-second shortcut examiners forget you know.

sections.heading: Polynomial Basics
bullets: Polynomial in x: aₙxⁿ + … + a₁x + a₀; degree = highest power; zero p(a) = 0 means (x − a) is a factor.
Remainder theorem: remainder of p(x) ÷ (x − a) is p(a). Example: p(x) = x³ − 2x² + x − 3 divided by (x − 1) → p(1) = −3.
Factor theorem: (x − a) is a factor iff p(a) = 0.
Relations for quadratic ax² + bx + c: sum of zeros = −b/a; product = c/a.

sections.heading: Identities
bullets: a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b); a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²); a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²).
a² + b² + c² − ab − bc − ca = ½[(a − b)² + (b − c)² + (c − a)²]; if a + b + c = 0 then a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc.
If x + 1/x = k: x² + 1/x² = k² − 2; x³ + 1/x³ = k³ − 3k. For k = 3 → 7 and 18.

sections.heading: Factorisation Methods
bullets: Common factor; grouping; splitting the middle term: x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3).
Using identities; trial for cubic using factor theorem (try ±1, ±2).

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Polynomials are factored using common factors, splitting, identities and the factor/remainder theorems.
keyFacts: a + b + c = 0 → a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc.

commonTraps: Do not forget sign errors in splitting.
